why_how.text: A clear view depends on what is in the sight line as well as seat adjustment. Mirror ornaments and decals should not be allowed to obstruct it.

Lens cleanliness and a working bulb are different parts of effective lighting. The recommendation includes headlights and rear or signaling lights; the recommendation includes the lamps that signal or show the vehicle as well as those lighting the road.
The settings are preparation for driving. Checking them while parked avoids starting with another person’s seating position or mirror view.
Seat height is about obtaining a usable forward view. A cushion is a listed aid when needed, not a reason to accept an obscured road view.
Visibility and control must both be considered. Improving one aspect of seating does not justify moving so close that the steering action becomes difficult.
The interior mirror is set for the rearward view through the back window. It has a different viewing role from the exterior side mirrors.
The slight forward lean is part of the described adjustment check. Keep it tied to the side-mirror view rather than substituting the interior mirror’s view.
The adjustable mirror needs to match the expected light. The existence of a setting does not remove the driver’s need to select it appropriately.
The restraint has a specific protective purpose in a rear impact. That purpose does not make it a substitute for a belt or a guarantee against every injury.
The location matters to the restraint’s intended job. The handbook connects the adjustment with the back of the head, not merely comfort elsewhere on the seat.

scenario.text: A learner faces this decision: What is the purpose of adjusting the seat height before driving?

reasoning.text: The proposed response is “To hide the road behind the dashboard.”. That alternative does not preserve the stated rule. Set the seat high enough to see the road clearly, using a cushion if needed.

result.text: Choose “To see the road clearly, using a cushion if needed.”. Keep the setting and every stated condition attached to that response.

claim.text: Common mistake: “To hide the road behind the dashboard.”.

correction.text: Set the seat high enough to see the road clearly, using a cushion if needed.

memory_support.text: Remember “Seat mirrors and visibility”. Connect the person or setting to the required action, then check the full statement for limits or exceptions.

prompt.text: Consider the earlier decision. Is “To hide the road behind the dashboard.” a sound response? Give the correction and explain the condition that decides it.

answer.text: Set the seat high enough to see the road clearly, using a cushion if needed.

rationale.text: The correction follows the stated rule rather than the proposed alternative. Set the seat high enough to see the road clearly, using a cushion if needed.

lines.text: Check the view, lighting and driver settings as separate tasks.

narration.text: Prepare the view and the controls before the vehicle moves. A mirror ornament or windshield decal can interfere with what the driver sees, while a dirty light lens can interfere with how effectively a lamp works. Seat and mirror settings also need attention before starting, especially after someone else has used the vehicle. These checks address different parts of preparation; one does not replace another. Raising the seat cannot remove a windshield obstruction, and a clear windshield does not show that the mirrors, lights or head restraint are correctly prepared for the driver.

lines.text: A working bulb and a clean lens are different checks.
Think about visibility from both directions.

narration.text: Think about visibility from both directions. The driver needs a clear line of sight through the windshield, so objects and decals should not obstruct it. The vehicle’s lights also need clean lenses, including lamps at the rear and lamps used for signaling or reversing. A bulb that illuminates does not settle whether dirt is reducing its usefulness. In a pretrip example, adjusting the seat while leaving an obstructing ornament in place solves only part of the problem. Work through the obstruction and lens checks rather than treating a single adjustment as complete preparation.

lines.text: A clearer view must not come at the expense of steering ability.
Seat position should support both seeing and steering.

narration.text: Seat position should support both seeing and steering. Increase the seating height enough to obtain a clear road view, using the listed cushion option if needed, but do not move so far forward that steering becomes difficult. Then set each mirror for its intended view: the interior mirror looks through the back window, while the side-mirror adjustment includes the slight forward-lean check described in the handbook. Match an adjustable mirror to the expected lighting too. These are preparation choices to make before driving, rather than adjustments to discover are wrong once in traffic.

lines.text: Connect the head restraint’s intended job with its adjustment.

narration.text: A head restraint is more than a seat feature to ignore once the driver feels comfortable. The handbook connects it with reducing whiplash in a rear impact and says to adjust it to contact the back of the head. Keep purpose and position together: knowing its intended job is useful only if the restraint is placed as described. That protective purpose is specific, so do not treat the restraint as a substitute for a safety belt or as a promise against every injury. Check its setting as part of preparing the driving position before the trip begins.

lines.text: Good seating supports a clear view and usable steering.

narration.text: A learner raises the seat to improve the forward view, then moves it so close that turning the wheel becomes difficult. Has the preparation succeeded? Only one goal has been addressed. The handbook pairs a useful road view with the warning against sitting too far forward for steering. The learner should preserve both requirements rather than choose between them. The same reasoning applies to the rest of the preparation: a correctly set interior mirror does not establish that the side mirrors, lighting setting or head restraint have also been checked. Each has its own described role.

lines.text: Keep the separate checks together before starting to drive.

narration.text: Use a before-moving routine to connect the pieces. Clear objects that obstruct the view, keep the vehicle’s light lenses clean, and check seat and mirror settings. For the seat, remember clear vision without crowding steering control. For the mirrors, remember the rear window, the side views and the expected lighting conditions. For the head restraint, remember the back-of-head adjustment and its rear-impact purpose. This is an organizing aid for the handbook’s separate checks, not a reason to omit one because another setting already feels comfortable or looks correct.

why_how.text: The handbook assigns a responsibility to the driver while retaining the listed legal exceptions. Personal passenger choices do not erase that stated driver responsibility.
The recommendation is not limited by trip length or low speed. Those common reasons for skipping a belt do not create an exception to the stated advice.
The check includes the driver and passengers and belongs before departure. Starting the trip is not the point at which restraint preparation should begin.
Door locking is included in the before-driving routine. It is a separate preparation step from fastening belts or adjusting mirrors.
The two portions belong to one protective system. Selecting only one does not preserve the intended use of the complete belt.
An automatic shoulder belt does not mean every part of the restraint has been fastened. The separate lap belt still needs attention.
Partial use is not equivalent to complete use. The handbook warns about reduced protection when only one portion of the system is worn.
Restraint use has consequences for nearby occupants as well as the person wearing it. A moving, unrestrained occupant can become part of the crash injury mechanism.

The listed older-vehicle exception is tied to manufacture date. It should not be expanded into an exception based on trip length, ownership or preference. Manufacture date does not become an exception for any vehicle a driver regards as old.
The stated exemption includes a documentation condition. A personal explanation or another passenger’s opinion does not replace the physician’s written statement described by the source.
The category and the operator matter. The source does not make ordinary work use or carrying equipment equivalent to operating a vehicle licensed as special mobile equipment.
The definition combines primary purpose with incidental highway movement. Merely using a vehicle for work does not establish the category described here.
Frequent official-duty stops are a basis for a possible agency exemption, not an automatic permission a driver creates. Preserve both the duty condition and agency role.
The form referral belongs to the frequent-stop exemption process. Its presence does not by itself grant an exemption or replace the Department of Justice decision.

scenario.text: A learner faces this decision: How should a two-part safety-belt system be used?

reasoning.text: The proposed response is “Wear only the shoulder portion every time.”. That alternative does not preserve the stated rule. A two-part belt system requires both the lap portion and the shoulder portion for its intended protection.

result.text: Choose “Wear both the lap and shoulder portions.”. Keep the setting and every stated condition attached to that response.

claim.text: Common mistake: “Wear only the shoulder portion every time.”.

correction.text: A two-part belt system requires both the lap portion and the shoulder portion for its intended protection.

memory_support.text: Remember “Belt use and exemptions”. Connect the person or setting to the required action, then check the full statement for limits or exceptions.

prompt.text: Consider the earlier decision. Is “Wear only the shoulder portion every time.” a sound response? Give the correction and explain the condition that decides it.

answer.text: A two-part belt system requires both the lap portion and the shoulder portion for its intended protection.

rationale.text: The correction follows the stated rule rather than the proposed alternative. A two-part belt system requires both the lap portion and the shoulder portion for its intended protection.

lines.text: Restraint checks belong before departure, including on short trips.

narration.text: Restraint preparation includes the driver and the other occupants. The handbook assigns the driver responsibility for proper belts or child seats, subject to listed legal exceptions, and places the belt and passenger check before departure. The recommendation to use a belt extends to short trips at low speed. A driver should therefore not wait for a fast road or a long journey before addressing restraints. Door locking is another departure step, while the belt system itself must be used as intended. Keep preparation, responsibility and the stated exceptions distinct rather than letting one erase the others.

lines.text: An automatic shoulder belt does not fasten a separate lap belt.
A lap-and-shoulder system is designed to be used as a complete system.

narration.text: A lap-and-shoulder system is designed to be used as a complete system. Wearing one portion does not provide the intended protection of both, and the handbook warns that protection is substantially reduced with partial use. This remains relevant when the shoulder portion moves automatically: the separate lap belt still needs to be buckled. In a pretrip check, seeing a shoulder belt in place should not end the check. Confirm the required lap portion as well, instead of assuming an automatic mechanism has completed every part of the occupant’s restraint preparation.

lines.text: An unrestrained person can also injure nearby people.
An unrestrained occupant can affect other people in the vehicle during a crash by striking
and seriously injuring them.

narration.text: An unrestrained occupant can affect other people in the vehicle during a crash by striking and seriously injuring them. That makes the passenger check more than a question about the unrestrained person’s own protection. The handbook places a responsibility on the driver to ensure proper restraints, while retaining the stated legal exceptions. Picture a driver who fastens a belt but does not check the passengers. The driver’s own preparation does not establish that the rest of the vehicle is ready. The departure routine needs to address the occupants as well as the driver.

lines.text: Different listed exemptions have different conditions.
Read an exemption as a defined condition, not a general permission to skip a belt.

narration.text: Read an exemption as a defined condition, not a general permission to skip a belt. The handbook’s older-vehicle exception is tied to manufacture date. The medical exception requires the occupant to carry a physician’s written statement. Those are different bases with different conditions, and neither becomes a short-trip or personal-preference exception. This lesson does not determine whether a particular person or vehicle qualifies. It teaches the distinction the source gives, without assuming that a personal explanation supplies the medical documentation or that a recent purchase changes a vehicle’s manufacture date.

title.text: Work use is not the category

lines.text: The licensed category and defined purpose matter.
The special-mobile-equipment exception is narrower than ordinary work use.

narration.text: The special-mobile-equipment exception is narrower than ordinary work use. The handbook identifies the operator of a vehicle licensed in that category and describes equipment whose primary purpose is not transporting people or property, with highway movement only incidental. Carrying tools or making a work trip does not by itself supply that definition. To understand the passage, connect the vehicle’s licensed category, its primary purpose and the operator named in the exception. Do not expand the exception to all workers, all equipment-carrying vehicles or every passenger in a work vehicle.

lines.text: A form referral is not an already granted exemption.

narration.text: Frequent stops during official job duties are another separately described situation. The handbook says the Department of Justice may grant an exemption and points workers to the named form. The word may and the agency’s role matter: deciding to make frequent stops does not create an exemption without that process. A form referral is a way to pursue the request, not proof that the request has already been granted. Keep this situation separate from the medical documentation condition and the special-mobile-equipment category rather than combining all exemptions into a single broad rule.

lines.text: Check the lap portion even when the shoulder portion moves automatically.

narration.text: A passenger sees an automatic shoulder belt move into place and decides that the loose lap belt can remain unused on a short trip. Identify both problems with that reasoning. The handbook still calls for buckling the lap portion, and short distance does not remove the advice to use the safety belt. Using only part of the system also reduces its protection. The driver’s before-departure check should therefore look at the actual restraint use rather than assume the mechanism or the planned route has already settled whether the occupant is properly prepared.

lines.text: Follow the preparation guidance without inventing broader exemptions.

narration.text: Keep three ideas in their own places. The departure routine includes fastening the driver’s belt, checking passenger restraints and locking the doors. The belt-use guidance calls for use on every trip and for both portions of a two-part system. The exception material describes particular conditions rather than a general choice to disregard that guidance. This structure helps avoid two opposite mistakes: ignoring an expressly listed condition, or inventing an exception because a journey seems short or a passenger finds one belt portion more convenient. The source gives conditions; personal preference does not add new ones.

why_how.text: The recommendation turns on proper fit, not just the label older child. The booster bridges the period before the adult belt fits the child correctly.
The words usually and about matter. The height is an approximate guide to fit, not a universal guarantee that every child fits a belt at an identical measurement.
The source keeps restraint type and belt use together. It does not turn the front-seat condition into permission to omit restraint components or substitute an adult’s arms.
Distance from the active airbag is an additional precaution in the stated front-seat situation. It does not replace proper restraint use.
The prohibition combines a rear-facing seat, a front passenger position and an active airbag. A short trip or the availability of a belt does not remove that stated restriction.
The recommendation combines the child’s age, restraint use and the back-seat location, with the source’s whenever-possible qualifier retained.
Passenger protection is individual. Sharing a belt does not provide the independent, properly used restraint described for each passenger.
An adult’s arms are not a substitute for the child’s independent restraint. The source identifies a crushing hazard during the collision, not a reliable protective role for holding the child.

scenario.text: A learner faces this decision: Where must a rear-facing child seat never be placed under the stated condition?

reasoning.text: The proposed response is “Only in a rear seat without an active front airbag.”. That alternative does not preserve the stated rule. Never put a rear-facing child seat in a front passenger position with an active airbag.

result.text: Choose “In a front passenger position with an active airbag.”. Keep the setting and every stated condition attached to that response.

claim.text: Common mistake: “Only in a rear seat without an active front airbag.”.

correction.text: Never put a rear-facing child seat in a front passenger position with an active airbag.

memory_support.text: Remember “Child and passenger protection”. Connect the person or setting to the required action, then check the full statement for limits or exceptions.

prompt.text: Consider the earlier decision. Is “Only in a rear seat without an active front airbag.” a sound response? Give the correction and explain the condition that decides it.

answer.text: Never put a rear-facing child seat in a front passenger position with an active airbag.

rationale.text: The correction follows the stated rule rather than the proposed alternative. Never put a rear-facing child seat in a front passenger position with an active airbag.

lines.text: A single age or height shortcut does not replace the other checks.

narration.text: Child passenger protection involves restraint fit, seating position and the way the restraint is used. The handbook recommends a booster for an older child until the adult lap-and-shoulder belt fits properly, and uses an approximate height as a usual fit guide. It also gives guidance about the back seat and cautions about a front position with an active airbag. These points should not be reduced to a single age or height shortcut. Each passenger still needs an independent, properly used restraint, so an adult holding a child or passengers sharing one belt does not supply the protection described.

title.text: Check fit rather than a label

lines.text: The height guidance is approximate; proper belt fit remains the condition.
An older child is not necessarily ready to use an adult belt without a booster.

narration.text: An older child is not necessarily ready to use an adult belt without a booster. The handbook ties the recommendation to proper lap-and-shoulder belt fit, while describing the usual height approximately rather than as a guarantee for every child. In a study example, the important question is not simply whether the child is older than before. It is whether the adult belt now fits properly. Preserve the words about and usually when remembering the height guidance, and do not turn an approximate indicator into a claim that checking the actual fit has become unnecessary.

lines.text: Moving a seat back does not remove the rear-facing-seat prohibition.
When the stated situation requires a child to sit in front, the handbook keeps the
restraint and the active airbag precautions together.

narration.text: When the stated situation requires a child to sit in front, the handbook keeps the restraint and the active airbag precautions together. It describes a child seat used with the vehicle belt or a booster used with the lap-and-shoulder belt, and says to move the seat as far back as possible. It separately prohibits a rear-facing child seat in a front passenger position with an active airbag. Moving the seat back does not cancel that prohibition. Read the conditions together instead of treating a single precaution as permission to disregard another one.

lines.text: A back-seat location does not replace a properly used restraint.

narration.text: Each passenger needs a restraint of their own, used properly. Sharing a belt or substituting an adult’s arms does not meet that independent-restraint idea. The handbook identifies a crushing risk when an adult holds a child during a collision, so the presence of a caring adult should not be mistaken for a restraint. It also recommends that children younger than thirteen be restrained in the back seat whenever possible. Keep location and restraint use together: choosing the back seat does not eliminate the need for the child’s properly used individual restraint.

title.text: Do not trade away a protection

lines.text: A separate precaution does not cancel a stated prohibition.

narration.text: A learner proposes placing a rear-facing child seat in front of an active passenger airbag, then moving the vehicle seat back to solve the problem. Does that preserve the handbook’s guidance? No. The front-seat distance precaution is separate from the stated prohibition on that rear-facing-seat location. The source does not present one as an exception to the other. A second shortcut would be to hold the child instead; that substitutes an adult’s arms for an independent restraint and introduces the crushing hazard the handbook identifies. Keep the different protections from being traded against one another.

lines.text: Check fit, position and proper individual restraint use.

narration.text: Review child passenger preparation as a set of connected decisions. Check whether the belt fits or a booster remains needed. Retain the handbook’s back-seat recommendation and its whenever-possible qualifier. If considering the stated front-seat situation, preserve the restraint pairing and airbag precautions, including the rear-facing-seat prohibition. Finally, confirm that every passenger has an independent, properly used restraint. This order is a recall aid for the source material, not a claim that one favorable condition makes every other condition irrelevant or that an adult can replace a restraint by holding the child.
